extracted.intended_audience: lobbyists, lobbying firms, in-house government affairs teams, compliance officers, and attorneys advising organizations on federal lobbying compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining who must register under the federal Lobbying Disclosure Act, how and when to file initial and quarterly disclosures (Forms LD-1 and LD-2), what must be reported, exemptions, and the enforcement/penalty framework for non-compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbyist definition (two-part test)
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual meets the definition of a lobbyist if they make more than one 'lobbying contact' and spend 20% or more of their time on 'lobbying activities' for a single client over a three-month period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both prongs must be satisfied (more than one lobbying contact AND >=20% time on lobbying activities for a single client in a three-month period) to qualify as a lobbyist for registration purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'lobbying contact'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Lobbying contact' is any oral or written communication to a covered official concerning federal policy, executive branch programs, or Senate confirmations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communications to 'covered officials' that concern the formulation, modification, or adoption of federal policies, legislation, or rules generally count as lobbying contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'lobbying activities'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Lobbying activities' include the preparation, planning, research, and other background work intended for use in lobbying contacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time spent on preparatory work intended to be used in communications with covered officials counts toward the 20% time threshold for lobbyist status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration responsibility (registrant liable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The obligation to register falls on the lobbying firm or the organization that employs the lobbyist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining who must file (outside lobbying firm vs. organization employing in-house lobbyists) is critical to compliance; registrant must ensure thresholds and definitions are correctly applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbying firm threshold for registration ($3,500)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lobbying firm working for outside clients must register if the total income from a client for lobbying activities is expected to exceed $3,500 in a quarterly period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate expected income from each client for the quarter; crossing the $3,500 threshold for a client triggers the registration obligation for the firm with respect to that client.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-house organization threshold for registration ($16,000)
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization employing its own in-house lobbyists must register if its total expenses for lobbying activities are expected to exceed $16,000 in a quarterly period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Total organizational lobbying expenses, not just individual lobbyist pay, are aggregated to determine whether the $16,000 quarterly threshold is met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial thresholds must coincide with individual lobbyist test
rubrics_metrics.description: The financial thresholds ($3,500 for firms, $16,000 for organizations) must be met alongside the individual lobbyist definition to trigger registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the monetary threshold and the individual-level lobbying-contact/time test must be considered before concluding registration is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial registration form and filing deadline (Form LD-1, 45 days)
rubrics_metrics.description: When thresholds are met, registrants must complete Form LD-1 and file electronically with the Clerk of the House and the Secretary of the Senate; the initial registration is due 45 days after a lobbyist first makes a lobbying contact or is retained to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File LD-1 electronically and track the 45-day clock from first contact or retention to avoid late-registration issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: LD-1 required disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Form LD-1 requires disclosure of the name of the client; a good faith estimate of the lobbying income or expenses that triggered registration; general issue areas expected to be lobbied; names of all employees who qualify as lobbyists; and identification of any organization contributing more than $5,000 toward lobbying activities that actively participates in planning or control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare accurate good-faith estimates and a complete list of lobbyists and contributing organizations; identify contributors who both give >$5,000 and actively participate in planning/control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quarterly reporting requirement (Form LD-2, 20-day deadline)
rubrics_metrics.description: After initial registration, registrants must file Form LD-2 quarterly detailing lobbying activities and financial information for the preceding calendar quarter; quarterly reports are due 20 days after the end of the calendar quarter (next business day if the 20th is a weekend/holiday).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calendarize reporting deadlines and account for weekend/holiday adjustments to avoid late filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: LD-2 financial reporting and rounding rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Form LD-2 requires a good faith estimate of total lobbying income received or total lobbying expenses incurred during the quarter, with amounts rounded to the nearest $10,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round reported amounts to the nearest $10,000 as required; use reasonable, documented methodology for the 'good faith' estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: LD-2 substantive activity disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Registrants must identify specific legislative or executive branch issues that were the subject of lobbying (including bill numbers, citations, or specific executive branch actions), the federal agencies or Houses of Congress contacted, and the names of individual lobbyists who engaged in the contacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific in describing issues (bill numbers, agency actions) and list individual lobbyists tied to each contact to satisfy disclosure granularity requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exempt communications (categories that do not count as lobbying contacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain communications do not count toward the registration thresholds, including: requests for status information; comments in response to a Federal Register public notice; testimony before a congressional committee; written comments filed in an administrative proceeding; and communications by members of the media in the course of gathering and disseminating news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a communication falls within an exemption before counting it as a lobbying contact; when in doubt, document the basis for treating a communication as exempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exempt entities and activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain entities/activities are generally exempt from disclosure: communications by religious organizations regarding their practices and beliefs; activities of state and local government officials acting in their official capacity; and certain communications related to legal proceedings that do not involve policy advocacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these entity/activity exemptions carefully—being a religious organization or state/local official does not automatically exempt all communications; the subject and context matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement process and cure period
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of the Senate and the Clerk of the House review filings; if a potential violation is detected the registrant is notified in writing and given 60 days to respond and correct the defect; failure to respond appropriately results in referral to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain good records and be prepared to respond within the 60-day cure period to avoid escalation to prosecutors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil penalties for knowing violations (up to $200,000)
rubrics_metrics.description: For knowing violations the LDA allows civil penalties up to a maximum of $200,000 for each violation, with fines determined based on the extent and gravity of the failure to register, report, or maintain accurate records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate recordkeeping and timely filings help mitigate risk; understand that fines are assessed per violation and consider materiality when evaluating exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal penalties for knowing and corrupt violations
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of a knowing and corrupt failure to comply with any provision of the Act, criminal penalties may be sought, including up to five years in prison or a fine under Title 18 of the United States Code, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentional, corrupt non-compliance carries severe criminal exposure—seek legal counsel if there is any risk of willful misconduct or allegation thereof.
